# What’s the Difference Between a Chef’s Knife and a Santoku?

These knives can tackle many of the same kitchen tasks, but they have some key differences.

[Saved](#save)

By [Carolyn Grillo](/authors/119-Carolyn-Grillo)

Published on March 14, 2023

When I first started working at America’s Test Kitchen, I owned a [chef’s knife](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2357-the-best-chef-s-knives-under-75), a [paring knife](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1800-paring-knives), and a [serrated knife](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2497-the-best-serrated-bread-knives). That’s it.

After spending time in the test kitchen and reading my colleague’s incredible knife reviews (everything from [boning knives](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1908-flexible-boning-knives) to [utility knives](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2145-serrated-utility-knives) to [bird’s beak paring knives](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2128-birds-beak-paring-knives)), I’ve filled out my collection with a few more.

Namely, a [santoku](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1815-santoku-knives).

A santoku is similar to a [chef’s knife](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2357-the-best-chef-s-knives-under-75)—both are supersharp with thin spines and are comfortable to hold and use. Plus, they tackle almost all of the same tasks in my kitchen. They’re both great for slicing mountains of onions for [French Onion Soup](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/4026-best-french-onion-soup), mincing up to 30 cloves of garlic for [aglio e olio](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/308-pasta-with-garlic-and-oil-aglio-e-olio), dicing and chopping vegetables for [Old-Fashioned Chicken Noodle Soup](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/10555-old-fashioned-chicken-noodle-soup), and beyond.

But there are a few key differences between [santoku knives](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1815-santoku-knives) and [chef’s knives](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2357-the-best-chef-s-knives-under-75), and what you choose to use in your kitchen comes down to personal preference.

## A Santoku Has a Shorter Blade

The blade of a [chef’s knife](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/2357-the-best-chef-s-knives-under-75) is typically between 8 and 10 inches long, while the blade of a [santoku](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1815-santoku-knives) is usually between 5 and 7 inches long. The shorter blade on a santoku knife can make users feel like they have more control.

Also, while santoku knives typically have a straighter bottom edge compared to the curved blade of a chef’s knife, some newer models have more rounded bottom edges, which allows for a full rocking motion.

## The Blade Tip of a Santoku Is More Rounded

Achef’s knife often has a more pointed, tapered tip while a santoku typically has a shorter, more rounded tip. This design is simply meant to make the knife look less intimidating and minimize the risk of piercing something unintentionally. In our [sanotku knife testing](https://www.americastestkitchen.com/equipment_reviews/1815-santoku-knives), we didn’t love the rounded tip, and preferred santoku knives that had tips that allowed them to function more like a chef’s knife.

## A Santoku Is (Usually) Lighter than a Chef’s Knife

Typically, but not always, a santoku knife is a bit lighter than a chef’s knife. A santoku’s lighter weight can help it feel more agile. In part, this has to do with the thinner blade spines—the top of the blade opposite the cutting edge. The thinner the blade spine the better, because it makes the blade feel more like a razor gliding through food than like a wedge pushing it apart.

One of our highly recommended santokus, the [Zwilling 7" Hollow Edge Rocking Santoku](https://shop.americastestkitchen.com/sale/exclusive-deals/knife-round-up-sale/zwilling-hollow-edge-rocking-santoku-knife.html?sourcekey=CARTZDAA0), has an interesting design, falling somewhere between a chef’s knife and a santoku, though it’s sold as a santoku.

This knife is the best of both worlds. It has the shorter blade length of a santoku (7 inches), but it also has a deeply curved cutting edge which allows you to “rock” like you’re using a chef’s knife. It also has a more pointed (not rounded) tip than most other santoku knives, which helps it get through food with less resistance.

### Straight to the Point

Our longtime favorite [Mac Hollow Edge Santoku Knife](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B000N5BV5K?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5122037%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) edged out the competition again, easily slicing through rubbery tomatoes, tender chives, tough carrots, and slick chicken skin.

I’ve tested many knives for Serious Eats, and among the coterie of Japanese blades ([nakiri](https://www.seriouseats.com/best-nakiri-knives-6931056), gyuto, and [deba](https://www.seriouseats.com/best-deba-knives-8304150), to name a few), santoku is one of the most approachable and versatile styles. It’s adept at slicing and dicing produce while also providing the agility to debone pieces of meat, like chicken thighs. Overall, it’s a home cook-friendly blade, which jives with its origin story.

“The Japanese modified the Western chef knife to become the gyuto, or ‘cow sword.’ Professional cooks who were preparing Western-influenced yoshoku food readily adopted the gyuto, but home cooks did not,” says Josh Donald of Bernal Cutlery. “It was too big and too different from the nakiri, deba, and yanagi home cooking setup. Knife-makers' response was to make a knife that would be more acceptable—smart and modern but not too much of a diversion from their mother's knife kit.” And thus the santoku knife was born. “Santoku were named either bunka-bocho (‘cultural knife’) or santoku (‘three virtues’) to give them a more respectful 'traditional' Japanese feel that wouldn't offend grandma,” Donald says.

To find the best santoku knives, I tested 19 of them by using them to slice tomatoes, dice carrots, mince chives, and break down chickens. My top picks are nimble, sharp, and versatile.

## The Tests

![a person using a santoku knife to break down a whole chicken]()

As part of our tests, we broke down whole chickens.


Serious Eats / Grace Kelly

* **Sharpness Tests:** I used the [Edge-On-Up Professional Edge Tester](https://www.sharpeningsupplies.com/products/edge-on-up-professional-edge-tester) to find the average sharpness reading of each knife before testing. (This is measured in grams of force needed to cut through a synthetic thread.) I then cut a piece of paper vertically with each knife to get an anecdotal idea of sharpness. After testing, I recorded the average sharpness again.
* **Tomato Test:** I used each knife to cut a tomato, noting if the blades sliced neatly through the skin.
* **Chive Test:** I minced a bundle of chives using each knife, noting if they crushed the tender herb or cut clean little rounds.
* **Carrot Test:** To examine how the knives handled hardier produce, I used each one to dice a carrot. Some wedged into the root vegetable and cracked it, while others diced neat cubes.
* **Chicken Test (Winners Only):** I used my favorite santoku knives to break down a whole chicken, noting their ability to cut through slippery chicken skin and to see if they could do detailed work around the joints.

## What We Learned

### What Is a Santoku Knife and What Is It Used For?

![a variety of santoku knives on a wodden cutting board with chives]()

Santoku knives have a unique, sheep's foot blade shape that distinguishes them from Western-style chef's knives.


Serious Eats / Grace Kelly

Santoku knives are everyday choppers. They’re great for slicing lean meats and cutting up produce. What makes them different from, say, a gyuto or [chef’s knife](https://www.seriouseats.com/the-best-chefs-knives) is their length (often between five and seven inches long) and their sheep’s foot form (a sloped tip that meets the bottom edge of the blade).

| Western Chef's Knife vs. Santoku Knife: A Quick Comparison | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ​ | **Western Chef’s Knife** | **Santoku Knife** |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Blade Length** | Six to 14 inches (six to eight inches is most typical) | Five to 7.5 inches |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bevel Angle** | 15 to 20 degrees | 10 to 12 degrees |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Edge Shape** | Curved blade belly that swoops upwards towards the tip | Sheep’s foot, where the knife's spine curves downward toward the tip |
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cutting Style** | Ideal for rock-chop motion | Ideal for push-cut motion |

The bottom edge is also often straighter than a Western-style chef’s knife, lending itself to a push-cut motion rather than a rocking chop. Santoku has a shallower blade angle than Western knives: 10 to 12 degrees is typical, versus the 15 to 20 degrees on a Western chef’s knife. And, as Donald explains, santoku often have a right-hand bias, which is something to consider if you’re a lefty.

“Santoku, like other ryoba (‘double-bevel’) knives, often have a right-hand bias either at the edge or on the face of the blade, but are not strictly right- or left-handed,” Donald says. “Asymmetrical blades (if they match the handedness of the user) will help the user do fine work, as the knife is hugging closer to what is being cut away from, but can lead the knife to pull to the inside while cutting something large. If you are lefty or will share it with a lefty, make sure there is not too much right-hand bias.”

Blade material varies among santoku knives. I tested carbon steel and stainless steel options, and choosing between them depends on your comfort level with [carbon steel blades](https://www.seriouseats.com/why-buy-carbon-steel-knives-best-kitchen-tools) and how much maintenance you’re willing to do yourself (read: [sharpening with a whetstone](https://www.seriouseats.com/best-knife-sharpeners)).

### Look for a Slightly Curved Blade

![two santoku knives, one with a straight edge blade and one with a curved blade, on a cutting board]()

Slightly curved blades made the push-cut motion feel more organic and smooth.


Serious Eats / Grace Kelly

While santoku knives are hardly as curved as a Western-style chef’s knife, I found the best ones did have a *slightly* curved blade. This gentle slope made the push-cutting motion feel smoother and more organic. Pin-straight blades, like on the [Lamson](https://www.amazon.com/Lamson-59953-Forged-Kullenschliff-Santoku/dp/B00ESH3L8Y?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5122037%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc), clunked against the cutting board. However, there’s such a thing as too much curve: The [Miyabi Artisan Rocking Santoku Knife](https://www.amazon.com/Miyabi-Rocking-Santoku-7-inch-Black/dp/B01MFD8SJN?tag=seriouseats-onsite-prod-20&ascsubtag=5122037%7C%7C%7C%7C%7C%7Cpc) felt less like a santoku and more like a [pizza-cutting mezzaluna](https://www.seriouseats.com/best-pizza-cutters-6830117).

### Slim, Light Knives Were Best

![a person holding a santoku knife over a cutting board with chives on it ]()

Slim, lightweight knives were more agile and adept at slicing deftly and precisely.


Serious Eats / Grace Kelly

Chopping produce shouldn’t dramatically tire your wrist and forearm. But some of the knives I tested were so heavy and thick that even slicing chives felt like more of a workout than a kitchen prep task. Although it was sharp, the [All-Clad](https://www.williams-sonoma.com/products/all-clad-santoku-knife-7-in/?pkey=s~santoku~69&position=29&sbkey=default) weighed nearly nine ounces, while the Lamson was close to 10. Both knives were far too heavy and unwieldy, and made cutting feel clunky. Instead, my favorite santoku knives were often between five and seven ounces and had thin blades that felt balanced with the handle. I felt in control with each slicing stroke.

### Carbon Steel vs. Stainless Steel Santoku Knives

![a carbon steel santoku on a wooden cutting board with chives]()

Carbon steel blades are more prone to splotches and rusting, but with proper care this can be mitigated.


Serious Eats / Grace Kelly

Whether you spring for a high carbon steel blade or stick with ol’ reliable stainless steel is up to you and how much care you want to put into your santoku. Carbon steel often starts out sharper and is easier to sharpen, but it is more brittle than stainless and needs to be thoroughly dried and rubbed with [mineral oil](https://www.seriouseats.com/mineral-oil-is-good-for-cutting-boards-and-knives) to prevent rusting. # Kitchen Knife Buying Guide

Updated November 24, 2021

A sharp kitchen knife is the single most important item in your culinary arsenal. It’s the only tool that can do everything from cutting up a whole chicken to finely mincing garlic or herbs. But [buying a great knife](https://www.consumerreports.org/chefs-knives/how-to-shop-for-a-chefs-knife-a5880897899/), or a great knife set, is tough. For starters, almost any knife is sharp when it’s new, a finding we confirmed in our last major test of kitchen knives, when the vast majority of models scored favorably for cutting performance.

Instead of getting hung up on a knife that’s simply sharp, hone in on construction, ergonomics, and feel, because along with how you [use and care for a chef’s knife](https://www.consumerreports.org/chefs-knives/how-to-use-and-care-for-a-chefs-knife-a1613029934/), those factors determine how a knife will hold up over time, and how easy it’ll be to use for repetitive cutting tasks day after day.

That’s exactly what we did in our most recent [test and assessment of eight chef’s knives](https://www.consumerreports.org/chefs-knives/best-chefs-knives-from-consumer-reports-tests-a1032926884/), which we conducted in our labs, as well as in our home kitchens. ## Parts of a Knife

**Bolster**  
A thick band of steel on forged knives. It helps balance the knife and protects your hands from accidental slips.

**Edge**  
The working part of the blade. The middle section cuts and slices. Advice: Before each use, hone the edge with a knife steel—a special, textured rod—to smooth and align a sharp edge. Sharpen the blade with a stone or other device to create a new edge when cutting becomes less precise. To gauge sharpness, cut paper down the edge. Hand-wash and dry the blade right after use to prevent corrosion.

**Handle**  
Choose a knife with an oval-shaped handle for the best ergonomics. Avoid knives with grooves, slots for fingers, or contours, because these are rarely ergonomic for a broad cross-section of users. Wood or metal handles provide a good grip, while plastic or synthetic handles can get slippery.

**Spine**  
The top of the blade, opposite the edge.

**Tang**  
The part of the blade that extends into the handle, the tang gives the knife balance.

**Tip**  
The forward quarter of the blade. It’s best for cutting small or delicate foods. The point is good for piercing. Advice: Don’t use the tip, or any other part of the knife, as a bottle opener or for other uses for which it’s not intended.

## What to Consider When Shopping for Kitchen Knives

**Focus on Essentials**  
You only need two knives in your kitchen—a chef’s knife and a serrated bread knife. The chef’s knife cuts just about anything, except for crusty bread, while the bread knife, well, you can probably guess. A small utility or paring knife is nice for items like strawberries, as are kitchen shears, which work for everything from twine to trimming a rotisserie chicken into pieces. But unless you’re committed to buying or building a full set, you can keep it to the basics.

**Consider Size**  
As the workhorse of the kitchen, the size of your chef’s knife needs some consideration. You’ll find most are between 6 and 10 inches. Shorter knives are easier to handle and control, but longer knives let you slice through larger foods, like a watermelon or a roast. For many, an 8-inch chef’s knife hits the sweet spot, which is why it’s the most common size you’ll find.

**Know the Terminology**  
Knives are forged or stamped. Forged knives, which tend to be higher priced, are created when a single piece of molten steel is cut and beaten into the desired shape. The blade is sturdy, with a heavy bolster, which is a flared piece of metal where the handle meets the blade, designed to protect the hand during cutting. Because forged blades are generally less flexible than stamped, they are less apt to bend over time.

Stamped knives, created by a cookie-cutter-type machine, are usually the same thickness throughout, except at the cutting edge, where they’re finer. They usually lack a bolster and heel. Stamped knives were historically cheaper, and considered to be inferior, but there are a few high-end companies that make premium stamped knives, including Global.

**Consider Composition**  
Steel is the metal used to form most knife blades, but not all steel is the same. Most knives use a combination of stainless steel and carbon steel, but in varying quantities. Stainless steel resists rust and corrosion, while carbon steel can take a better edge. Look for a knife that offers "high-carbon stainless steel" if you want to blend the best of both metals.

**Hold the Handle**  
The best way to get a feel for a knife is to use it, or at the very least, grip the handle in the store. Some retailers, like Williams-Sonoma and Sur La Table, have return policies that allow you to exchange a knife 30 to 60 days after purchase. Take a new knife for a test run in your own kitchen, to make sure it’s comfortable, easy to control, and doesn’t cause cramping while you cut.

### Knife Brands to Know

Most premium knives hail from Germany or Japan. German manufacturers make mostly European-style knives, which often feature thicker blades and a large bolster. Many Japanese manufacturers opt for a thinner blade and a finer edge. The brands featured here include many that CR has [tested](https://www.consumerreports.org/products/kitchen-knives-31111/kitchen-knives-31095/view2/) in the past, or which we recently reviewed with our in-house ergonomics expert.

Chicago Cutlery

A large manufacturer of inexpensive cutlery, sold at major retailers like Amazon, Bed Bath & Beyond, Macy’s, and Walmart.


Cutco

A large company that uses direct-to-consumer and multilevel marketing to sell knives. Though these knives often come with fairly premium prices, they include a lifetime warranty. Their signature handle features large indentations or grooves, which our experts say isn’t ideal when designing a knife that will provide an ergonomic grip.


Global

Global makes Japanese cutlery in Yoshikin, Japan, using a blend of high-carbon stainless steel. Its knives feature modern, dimpled metal handles that are oval in shape, which is naturally ergonomic, but handles are on the small side, so large-handed users especially may want to try them before buying.


J.A. Henckels

J.A. Henckels has been making premium knives in Solingen, Germany, for around 300 years, now using a mix of high-carbon stainless steel. In addition to high-end knives, it also makes more mass-market knives, sold at lower prices, in stores like Bed Bath & Beyond and Kohl’s.


Keemake

Keemake is a company that makes Japanese-style knives sold almost exclusively on Amazon. It offers great styling at low prices, but our testing has found design lacking when it comes to ergonomics.


KitchenAid

Best known for its stand mixers and other small appliances, KitchenAid also makes licensed cutlery and chef’s knives at entry-level prices.


Mac

Mac is an American knife company that manufactures knives in Japan. It’s known for using an exceptionally high-carbon blend of stainless steel in their construction. Its products are geared toward chefs and professionals and are sold online.


Mercer

Mercer is a manufacturer that uses German and Japanese steel to produce premium knives sold online on its own website, as well as on Amazon.


Shun

Shun is a 20-year-old knife company that makes premium, Japanese-style knives sold at high-end retailers like Williams-Sonoma.


Wusthof

Like J.A. Henckels, Wusthof makes premium European-style knives in Solingen, Germany, using high-carbon stainless steel. Its knives tend to be premium, with no entry-level offerings, and are sold online as well as in high-end retail stores.


Zyliss

A brand best known for small kitchen gadgets like potato peelers, Zyliss makes entry-level knives for home cooks.
